title: Satta and Balvand
hook: two minstrels who, tradition says, quarreled with Guru Arjan and were forgiven; their Var is in the Granth (Ramkali, ang 966–968)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bhatts, who praised the Gurus as one light. Your line was poets of praise. Did you tell someone the goodness you'd seen in them? Day seven hundred ninety-two.

Two musicians, a rebab and a voice, singing kirtan in the Guru's court. Satta and Balvand. Then, tradition says, something goes wrong. A request for money, a quarrel, wounded pride. They stop singing. They say hard things about the house they served. And they walk out. A falling-out could end right there. This one ends with their song inside the Guru Granth Sahib, in Raag Ramkali, Ang 966, kept and sung beside the Gurus' own words.
screen: `TWO MUSICIANS IN THE GURU'S COURT.` → `A QUARREL, AND A WALKOUT.` → `THEIR SONG IN THE GRANTH.`

segments.voice: First the story, as tradition tells it. Satta and Balvand ask Guru Arjan for help, and when it isn't what they hoped, pride takes over. They refuse to play, and they boast that the Gurus' fame rests on their music. Without the court, though, their fortunes sink. In the end they come back, humbled, asking forgiveness, and tradition says a devoted Sikh pleaded for them. The Guru forgives them. They pick up the rebab again. That's the tradition. Now the text, which is what the Granth actually keeps: their Var, a ballad, in Raag Ramkali. And what does it sing about? Not themselves. It sings about Guru Nanak setting up Lehna as the next Guru, Guru Angad, and the line passing on. In paraphrase, one of its lines: the light is the same, the way is the same; the master has only changed the body. It's the claim the Bhatts made yesterday, but listen to who is making it now. Two men who once claimed the Gurus needed them end up singing that the Guru is one light, needing nothing from anyone, passing from body to body. The quarrel was about who mattered. The song answers it: the light matters, and everyone else is a singer. And notice what the Guru did. He didn't just let them back in the door. Their words went into the scripture, to be sung in gurdwaras alongside his own. Forgiveness here isn't a grudging truce. It's a microphone handed back.
screen: `A REQUEST, A QUARREL, A WALKOUT.` · `HUMBLED, THEY COME BACK; THE GURU FORGIVES.` · `THE SAME LIGHT, ONLY THE BODY CHANGED.` · `A MICROPHONE HANDED BACK.` · then, large: `FORGIVEN, AND SUNG.`

segments.voice: The practice: forgive a quarrel. In the sit, choose a small one. Not the deepest wound of your life; something sized for two minutes. A sharp exchange, a slight, a door that closed. Let the other person's face come to mind. You don't have to call them, and you don't have to pretend it didn't happen. Just loosen your grip on it, one breath at a time. If something in you is ready, imagine handing them their voice back. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Var. A ballad: Satta and Balvand's, in Raag Ramkali, singing that the light is the same, the way is the same, only the body has changed.
Your line: forgiven, and sung. Today, once, let someone who stepped on your toes back into the conversation, and let them speak. Day seven hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: The Var of Satta and Balvand in Raag Ramkali is sung in kirtan like other Gurbani, and Sikhs tell their story as one of pride, return and forgiveness.

options: forgive them, but never let them sing again.
forgive them, and keep their song in the scripture.
fork.reveal: tradition says Guru Arjan forgave them, and their Var is in the Granth, sung alongside the Gurus' own words.

original.note: Gurmukhi: a ballad; the Var of Satta and Balvand is set in Raag Ramkali.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about two musicians who got in trouble.
what it means: they quarreled, came back and were forgiven, and their Var sings that the Guru is one light.
what a scholar hears: the quarrel is tradition; the text is the Var itself, whose line about the same light in a changed body is a key witness to the Guruship passing on.

sources.ref: Ramkali ki Var, Satta and Balvand, Ang 966–968

notes: The quarrel story (request for help, refusal to play, boasting, decline, return, intercession by a devoted Sikh, traditionally Bhai Ladha of Lahore) is attributed to tradition; the intercessor is left unnamed. Confirm.
Paraphrase of 'joti ohaa jugat saai sahi kaaiaa pher palateeai': confirm wording and 'one of its best-known lines' (softer phrasing may be preferred).
The Var's subject (Guru Nanak installing Lehna as Guru Angad, and the succession) is summarized; the Var also praises later Gurus. Confirm.
'Sung in gurdwaras alongside his own' is general; confirm.
Index places Satta and Balvand under 'the other Bhagats'; they are minstrels (rababis), not Bhagats, which the script reflects.
Editor pass: tied the Var's 'same light' line explicitly to yesterday's Bhatts so it reads as a new witness, not a repeat, and varied the hook ending and practice opener.
Audit (2026-10-01): checked; the joti ohaa jugat saai line is correctly placed in the Var, the quarrel stays framed as tradition, and the link to the Bhatts reads as a new witness. No change.
